title: English with Kyle
topic: Business Letter Translation / Past Continuous / Phrasal Verbs

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up: Past Continuous
sections.content:
Used for actions **in progress** when something else happened (interruption) or for **simultaneous** past actions.

Structure: **was/were + verb-ing**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Qué pasó cuando venías aquí? | What happened when you were coming here? |
| Le vi cuando iba a clase | I saw him when he was going to class |
| ¿Qué hacías cuando les viste? | What were you doing when you saw them? |
| ¿A dónde ibas cuando tuviste el accidente? | Where were you going when you had the accident? |
| Bajaba de su coche cuando la bomba estalló | He was getting out of his car when the bomb went off |
| Pensaba en ti cuando me llamaste | I was thinking about you when you called me |
| Cuando me di cuenta del error, ya se iba | When I realized my mistake, he was already leaving |

> **“What did it happen?”** ✗ — When asking for the **subject**, no auxiliary is needed: **“What happened?”** ✓

---

### By the time

*Para cuando* — one thing finished before the other was complete.

- **By the time** I realized my mistake, he was already leaving.
- **By the time** the bus came, we were already late.
- **By the time** our flight arrived, the taxis had already gone.

sections.title: 2. Phrasal Verbs: Get & Blow
sections.content:
### Get into / Get out of — enclosed spaces

Use with **cars, taxis, elevators**:

- **Get into** the car · **Get out of** the car
- **Get into** a taxi · **Get out of** an elevator

### Get on / Get off — large vehicles

Use with **buses, planes, trains**:

- **Get on** the bus · **Get off** the bus
- **Get on** the plane · **Get off** the train

> Things you **get into**, you **get out of**. Things you **get on**, you **get off**.

---

### Blow / Go Off / Put Out

| Expression | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| The bomb **went off** | La bomba estalló | *The bomb went off at midnight.* |
| The building **blew up** | El edificio voló por los aires | *The explosion blew up the building.* |
| **Blow out** a candle | Apagar soplando | *Blow out your birthday candles.* |
| **Put out** a fire | Apagar un incendio | *Firefighters put out the fire.* |

> A bomb **goes off**. A building **blows up**. Candles are **blown out**. Fires are **put out**.

sections.title: 3. Think About / Think Of / Think Up
sections.content:
Three related but distinct expressions:

| Expression | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Think about** | Pasar un rato con algo en la cabeza | *I was thinking about you / about hamburgers.* |
| **Think of** | In the middle — slight implication of invention | *I thought of a solution last night while washing the dishes.* |
| **Think up** | Pure invention / idear | *We need to think up a new recipe for the greatest burger ever.* |

> **Think about** = just having something in your mind, no invention implied.
>
> **Think up** = purely creative — *we need to think up a plan.*
>
> **Think of** = somewhere in between; the idea *appeared* — *I can’t think of the word right now.*

sections.title: 4. Notice vs. Realize
sections.content:
| Expression | Spanish | Type |
|---|---|---|
| **To notice** | Fijarse — con los sentidos | Sensory awareness — less cerebral |
| **To realize** | Darse cuenta | Mental processing — more cerebral |

**Example sequence:**
> *I noticed a strange smell* → sensory, external
> *Then I realized my neighbor was smoking.* → mental processing, understanding the cause

- **Notice** = becoming aware **through the senses** (sight, smell, sound)
- **Realize** = **understanding** what something means, processing consequences

> Notice is less cerebral — it’s external. Realize involves insightfulness — you process what it *means*.

sections.title: 5. Business Letter: Formal English  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
### Letter

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| A quien corresponda, | To whom it may concern, |
| Les escribo porque he sufrido daños personales a causa de un producto defectuoso fabricado por su empresa. | I am writing to you because I have suffered personal injury due to a defective product manufactured by your company. |
| Esta mañana decidí probar su nueva y "revolucionaria" cuchilla de afeitar de seis hojas (six-blade razor), The Six Drive. He sido un fiel cliente suyo durante más de 30 años y he empezado a dar por sentado no sólo el carácter innovador de sus productos, sino también su alta calidad. | This morning I decided to try out your new "revolutionary" six-blade razor, The Six Drive. I have been a loyal customer of yours for over 30 years and have started to take for granted not only the innovative nature of your products, but also their high quality. |
| Así que podrán imaginar mi decepción y enfado cuando, después de haberme afeitado, mi cara parecía como si hubiera sido atacada salvajemente por un gato psicópata. Cuando examiné la cuchilla con la que me había rasurado, vi que dos de las hojas estaban partidas por la mitad. Por culpa de estas hojas rotas tengo la cara cubierta de arañazos y tengo suerte de no haber sufrido lesiones mayores. Adjunto fotos de mi cara y de la cuchilla culpable. | So you will be able to imagine my disappointment and anger when, after shaving, my face looked as if it had been savagely attacked by a psychopathic cat. When I examined the blade I had shaved with, I found that two of the blades were broken in half. Due to these broken blades my face is covered in scratches and I am lucky not to have suffered more serious injuries. I enclose photos of my face and the offending blade. |
| ¿Qué piensan hacer para compensarme por este desafortunado suceso? | What do you intend to do to make up for this unfortunate incident? |
| Atentamente, | Yours sincerely, |

---

A complaint letter translated from Spanish, practising key formal English phrases.

---

### Key phrases and vocabulary

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| A quien corresponda | **To whom it may concern** |
| Defectuoso | **Defective** / **faulty** |
| Cliente (compra producto) | **Customer** |
| Cliente (compra servicio) | **Client** |
| Dar por sentado | **To take for granted** |
| Más de 30 años | **Over** 30 years *(more natural than “more than”)* |
| Probar algo nuevo | **To try out** |
| Intentar | **To try** |
| Compensar | **To compensate** / **to make up for** |
| Como si | **As if** |
| Arañazos | **Scratches** |
| Adjunto dentro del sobre | **Enclosed** |
| Adjunto al email | **Attached** |
| El culpable (un objeto) | **The offending** — *the offending blades* |

---

### Grammar notes

**Who vs. Whom:** Grammar books say use *whom* for objects, but in real life almost nobody does — except **“To whom it may concern.”**

**“Will can” does not exist →** use **“will be able to”:**
> *You’ll be able to imagine my anger.*

**Enclosed vs. Attached:**
- *Enclosed* = inside the envelope / embedded in the email body.
- *Attached* = a separate file annexed to the email (like a PDF).

**Customer vs. Client:**
- *Customer* = someone who buys a **product**.
- *Client* = someone who buys a **service**.

**Try vs. Try out:**
- *Try* = intentar (*I tried to climb the wall but I couldn’t.*)
- *Try out* = probar algo nuevo (*I decided to try out your new razor.*)

**Defective vs. Faulty:** both mean *defectuoso*. *Faulty* comes from *fault* (falta/defecto).

| **the offending X** | El X culpable (for objects, not people) — *the offending blades* |

| **scratches** | Arañazos |
| **to rush** | Ir con prisa — *they rushed into the store* |

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Según él, deberías haberlo hecho | According to him, you should have done it |
| Hay un viejo dicho sobre ese tema | There's an old saying about that subject |
| En cuanto a mí se refiere | As far as I'm concerned *(you can do whatever you want)* |
| Si fueras un poco más optimista | If you were a little more optimistic |
| Soy pesimista por naturaleza | I'm a pessimist / I'm pessimistic |
| Todos a favor del plan que levanten la mano | All in favor of the plan, raise your hand |
| Se fue por el desagüe | It went down the drain |
| ¿Qué harás cuando te jubiles? | What will you do when you retire? |
| Haré un viaje alrededor del mundo | I'll take a trip around the world |

> **Vocabulary:** *to gurgle* — the sound water makes going down a drain. Informal: *it went down the gurgler.*

> **Trip vs. Travel:** *travel* is the verb (*we traveled to Rome*); *trip* is the noun and needs another verb — *to take a trip, to go on a trip* (*not* ~~to trip to Rome~~).

sections.title: 2. What does he look like? / How does he look? / What is he like?  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
Two dimensions to consider: **physical appearance** vs. **personality**, and **permanent/fact** vs. **temporary/opinion**.

| | Physical appearance | Personality |
|---|---|---|
| Permanent / fact | **What does he look like?** | **What is he like?** |
| Temporary / opinion | **How does he look?** | **How is he?** |

---

### Physical appearance

**What does he look like?** — permanent, factual description

- What does your brother look like? → *He's tall and has gray hair.*
- What did your grandfather look like? → *He was tall and strong and had gray hair.*
- What will the city look like after the renovations?
- What does Santa Claus look like? → *He's fat and wears a red suit.*

> Answer with **to be** or **to have** — never *he looks like tall* ✗

**How does he look?** — temporary, invites an opinion

- How did he look when you saw him? → *He looked tired / ill / different.*
- How does she look? → *She looks much healthier than before.*

---

### Personality

**What is he like?** — permanent character traits

- What is your brother like? → *He's hardworking, stubborn, and very generous.*
- What was your grandmother like? → *She was strict but loving.*

**How is he?** — temporary mood or state

- How is your neighbour these days? → *He's much more relaxed than he used to be.*
- How was John when you saw him? → *He was in a great mood.*

---

> **Rule of thumb:** *What* asks for facts/descriptions. *How* asks for opinion or current state. *Like* = permanent. No *like* = temporary.

sections.title: 3. Negative Comparisons: not as many / not as much
sections.content:
Convert **fewer / less** sentences into **not as many / not as much**.

| Type | Direct comparison | Negative comparison |
|---|---|---|
| Countable | There are **fewer** horses in Portugal than in Spain. | There are **not as many** horses in Portugal **as** in Spain. |
| Uncountable | There is **less** water in Jordan than in Canada. | There is **not as much** water in Jordan **as** in Canada. |
| Countable | There are **fewer** languages spoken in Finland than in Africa. | There are **not as many** languages spoken in Finland **as** in Africa. |
| Uncountable | There is **less** sand in Andorra than in Egypt. | There is **not as much** sand in Andorra **as** in Egypt. |
| Countable | There are **fewer** olive trees in Galicia than in Andalusia. | There are **not as many** olive trees in Galicia **as** in Andalusia. |

> The negative form (*there isn't as much / there aren't as many*) is very common in natural speech — more so than the positive *there is as much*. Worth mastering.

**Key:** *as many* = countable (fewer ↔ not as many) · *as much* = uncountable (less ↔ not as much)

sections.title: 4. Grammar Notes
sections.content:
### Noun vs. adjective: pessimist / pessimistic

| Form | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Noun | I'm **a pessimist** | Needs the article |
| Adjective | I'm **pessimistic** | No article |
| Adjective + noun | I'm **a pessimistic person** | Article goes with the noun |

---

### Raise vs. Rise

| Verb | Type | Forms | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Raise** | Transitive (needs object) | raise / raised / raised | I am **raising** my hand. The government **raises** taxes. |
| **Rise** | Intransitive (no object) | rise / **rose** / **risen** | My hand is **rising**. Taxes **rise**. |

> *I raise the phone → the phone rises.* Same event, two verbs depending on whether there is a subject performing the action.

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
**Direct & Indirect Object Pronouns**

When a pronoun replaces the object, the word order changes — the preposition **to** is required:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Explícamelo una vez más | Explain it to me one more time *(not "explain me it")* |
| Kyle le está dando el libro a Pepe | Kyle is giving Pepe the book → He is giving **it** to **him** |

---

**Translation practice from class**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Fue mucho más fácil que la última vez | It was much easier than the last time |
| ¿Cuánto tardó? | How long did it take you? *(subject = "it")* |
| Él estaba mejor preparado que yo | He was better prepared than me / than I was |
| Vino el fontanero para mirarlo | The plumber came to look at it |
| Se estaban quejando de la falta de un plan concreto | They were complaining about the lack of a concrete plan |
| Pero vieron esto, ¿no? | But they saw this, **didn't they**? |

> **Vocabulary note:** *plumber* has a **silent B** — another example: *crumbs*.

sections.title: 2. Question Tags
sections.content:
Take the **auxiliary verb**, flip it (affirmative → negative or negative → affirmative), then repeat the subject pronoun.

| Sentence | Tag |
|---|---|
| It is important… | …isn't it? |
| You like coffee… | …don't you? |
| He likes fish… | …doesn't he? |
| He was here yesterday… | …wasn't he? |
| They can't fix it… | …can they? |
| But they saw this… | …didn't they? |

> With the verb **to be**, it acts as its own auxiliary — no extra verb needed.
>
> In Canadian English, people informally say **"eh?"** instead of a proper tag (not standard, but common).

sections.title: 3. Picture Vocabulary
sections.content:
Verbs and phrases practised from images:

| Image | Expression |
|---|---|
| Man looking in mirror | He's **shaving** *(we don't say "shaving himself")* |
| Two men greeting | They're **bowing** / They're **shaking hands** |
| Man with camera | He's **taking a photo** / **taking a picture** · The camera is **flashing** |
| Sunrise/sunset scene | The sun is **rising** / **setting** over the desert |
| Crowd entering a store | They're **rushing into** the store / They're **crashing the door** *(Black Friday)* |
| People in the rain | They're **taking shelter** under a palm leaf |
| Person with gift | She/he is **wrapping a gift** / **wrapping a present** · **wrapping paper** |

**Extra vocabulary:**
- **A sale / on sale** — something sold at a reduced price
- **Door crash deal** — a special offer only for the first people through the door (Black Friday term)
- **Mixed reviews** — some people liked it, some didn't *(taquilla = box office)*

sections.title: 4. Comparatives with as…as  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
### Basic structure: **as … as** / **not as … as**

*tan … como / no tan … como*

- Valencia is **not as big as** Madrid
- I'm **not as tall as** my brother
- English is **not as difficult as** Chinese

---

### 1. Not quite as … as — *small gap, close comparison*

> Implies the two things are **almost the same** but one falls slightly short.

- It's **not quite as** salty **as** last time *(casi igual de salado)*
- The museum wasn't **quite as** interesting as we hoped
- The exam wasn't **quite as** difficult as I thought it would be
- Barcelona isn't **quite as** big as Madrid
- My house isn't **quite as** big as my brother's
- The film is **not quite as** good as the book
- His second book is **not quite as** interesting as the first
- Málaga's beaches aren't **quite as** long as Cádiz's

---

### 2. Not nearly as … as — *large gap, big difference*

> Implies there is a **significant** difference — one thing is much less than the other.

- I'm **not nearly as** fast as Usain Bolt *(con mucha diferencia)*
- Trujillo isn't **nearly as** big as Madrid
- This cover isn't **nearly as** good as the Beatles original
- His desk isn't **nearly as** untidy as hers
- The film isn't **nearly as** good as the book
- My hometown is **not nearly as** crowded as Madrid
- It doesn't have **nearly as much** traffic as Madrid *(countable/uncountable applies: as much / as many)*

---

### Quick comparison

| Expression | Spanish equivalent | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| not quite as … as | no tan … como *(casi)* | Small — almost equal |
| not nearly as … as | ni con mucho tan … como | Large — clearly less |

---

### 3. Just about as … as — *almost equal, barely reaches*

> Like saying *casi* — it's right there, very close.

- I'm **just about as** good as him at tennis *(casi tan bueno como él)*
- My brother is taller but I'm **just about as** tall
- My mother's cooking is **just about** the best in the world
- My grandmother was **just about** the most cheerful person I've ever known
- It's **just about** the best burger in town

---

### 4. Just about to — *on the verge of doing something*

> Means *a punto de hacer algo* — you were very close to doing it but didn't.

- I was **just about to** call you *(a punto de llamarte)*
- He was **just about to** open the window when it started pouring
- That's what I was **just about to** say
- I was **just about to** go out when you called me
- I was just about to warn you when the ceiling fell

> **Note:** this is different from *just about + adjective* above — same words, different meaning depending on context.

sections.title: 5. Weather Vocabulary
sections.content:
| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| to **pour** / it's **pouring** | diluviar | *It started pouring rain.* |
| to **drizzle** / it's **drizzling** | chispear, lloviznar | *I love Paris when it's drizzling.* |
| to **sprinkle** / it's **sprinkling** | llovizna muy ligera | *It's just sprinkling — no need for an umbrella.* |

> **Sprinkler** — a device that sprinkles water; used in buildings as a fire safety system.
>
> *Drizzle* is also used in cooking: *drizzle olive oil over the salad* = echar un chorrito de aceite.

title: English with Kyle
topic: Spot the Differences · I Wish (Present & Past Regrets)

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hay algo suelto en el sobre. | There's something loose in the envelope. |
| El tornillo está demasiado flojo. | The screw is too loose. |
| Es un lugar muy solitario. | It's a very lonely place. |
| La música está demasiado alta. | The music is too loud. |
| Hicieron un trabajo chapucero. | They did a lousy job. / They did a sloppy job. |
| Ella tiene una voz encantadora. | She has a lovely voice. |
| Ha sido una experiencia significativa. | It has been a meaningful experience. |
| Estas cifras no significan nada para mí. | These figures are meaningless to me. |
| Estás equivocado. | You're mistaken. / You're wrong. |
| Soy un poco miope. | I'm a little near-sighted. |
| Sería una experiencia dolorosa para todo el mundo. | It would be a painful experience for everyone. |
| Pepe es una persona extrovertida. | Pepe is an outgoing person. / Pepe is an extroverted person. |

**Key notes:**

- **Loose vs. lose vs. lost:** *loose* (flojo, L-O-O-S-E, adjective) · *lose* (perder, L-O-S-E, verb) · *lost* (perdido, past participle). Easy to mix up — different spelling and meaning.
- **Lousy / sloppy:** both translate *chapucero* — *a lousy job* / *a sloppy job*.
- **-ful / -less opposite pairs:** *meaningful ↔ meaningless*, *painful ↔ painless*, *careful ↔ careless*. But not every pair works this way — **helpful** (it helps others) and **helpless** (it can't help itself) are *not* true opposites.
- **Compound adjectives take a hyphen:** two words joined into one adjective, like *near-sighted*, always get a hyphen (*guión medio*).
- **Needle vs. jab:** *needle* is the everyday word for an injection; British English often says *get the jab*.

sections.title: 2. Spot the Differences — Descriptive Vocabulary
sections.content:
A find-the-differences picture exercise, describing two nearly identical living-room scenes in full English sentences.

**Useful vocabulary that came up:**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **fireplace** | where the fire burns (not *chimney* — *chiminea* → *fireplace*) |
| **chimney** | where the smoke goes out |
| **hearth** (H-E-A-R-T-H) | the brick/stone area inside a fireplace |
| **bowl** (B-O-W-L) | container for fruit, etc. |
| **globe** | spherical model of the Earth — not *"global sphere"* |
| **rug** | covers *part* of the floor (*alfombra*) |
| **carpet** | typically covers the *entire* floor (*moqueta*) |
| **collar** | around an animal's neck |
| **scarf / blanket** | draped over furniture |

**Grammar notes:**

- **into vs. in:** *into* shows movement (*someone put the apples into the bowl*); *in* shows the resulting static location (*the apples are in the bowl*).
- **Avoid the redundant pronoun:** don't say *"the frame it's different"* — *it's* repeats the subject that's already there. Just say **"the frame is different."**

sections.title: 3. Grammar: I Wish — Present & Future Unreal Wishes
sections.content:
*I wish* works like a conditional: it always steps back one verb tense from what you'd normally expect, because it describes something hypothetical or impossible — not real.

**Present unreal wish → I wish + past simple:**

> *I wish I were taller.*
> *I wish I knew more languages.*
> *I wish I spoke perfect Spanish.*

❌ *I wish I speak perfect Spanish* — never use the present simple after *wish*.

**With the verb *to be*, always use *were*, never *was* — it's the subjunctive form:**

> *I wish I were rich.* (not ~~I wish I was rich~~)
> *If I were you...* (same subjunctive rule)

**More examples (it's a pity / it's a shame + present fact → I wish + past simple):**

| Spanish cue | English with *I wish* |
|---|---|
| Es una pena que no sepa reparar la máquina. | I wish he knew how to repair the machine. |
| Es una pena que no haya más oportunidades. | I wish there were more opportunities. |
| Es una pena que no haya solución al problema. | I wish there were a solution to the problem. |

**Short answers with *wish* — go back one step, just like the auxiliary in a normal short answer:**

| Question | Short answer + wish |
|---|---|
| Am I rich? | No, I'm not, but I wish I were. |
| Can you turn invisible? | No, I can't, but I wish I could. |
| Is gasoline cheap in Spain? | No, it isn't, but I wish it were. |
| Is there an easy way to get rich? | No, there isn't, but I wish there were. |

**Wish vs. hope:** use *hope* when there's still real possibility in the future (*Will you know it perfectly someday? I hope I will*). Use *wish* for something hypothetical or unreal.

sections.title: 4. Grammar: I Wish — Past Regrets & Short Answers
sections.content:
When *it's too bad / it's a pity / it's a shame* refers to something that already happened, *I wish* steps back to the **past perfect** to express regret.

| Spanish cue / situation | English with *I wish* |
|---|---|
| Es una lástima que perdieran el partido. | I wish they had won the match. / I wish they hadn't lost the match. |
| Es una pena que perdiera su DNI. | I wish he hadn't lost his ID. |
| Es una pena que se rindieran tan pronto. | I wish they hadn't given up so soon. |
| No pudo ir al concierto. | I wish he could have attended the concert. / I wish he had been able to attend the concert. |

**Short answers, past version — go back to *had*:**

| Question | Short answer + wish |
|---|---|
| Did you win the Christmas lottery last year? | No, I didn't, but I wish I had. |
| Did you master this yesterday? | No, I didn't, but I wish I had. |

**Quick reference — how far back *wish* goes:**

| Question tense | Wish tense |
|---|---|
| am / is / are (present) | were |
| can | could |
| simple past (did) | had + past participle |

> *It's a problem, but I wish it weren't.*
> *I wish I weren't so stubborn.*

title: English with Kyle
topic: Phrasal Verbs with Put · Unless · What vs. How (Senses)

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Dónde conseguiste eso? | Where did you get that? |
| ¿Cómo voy a ayudarte si no me dejas? | How am I going to help you if you don't let me? |
| Llevo dos años trabajando aquí. | I've been working here for two years. |
| Tienes que tener cuidado con ellos. | You have to be careful with them. |
| Mi jefe tiene un acento británico. | My boss has a British accent. |
| Se te cayó. | You dropped it. |
| Me encanta mezclar bebidas. | I love to mix drinks. / I love mixing drinks. |
| ¿Cómo puedes beber tanta cerveza? | How can you drink so much beer? |

**Key notes:**

- **To get** — "the king of verbs" (*el rey de los verbos*): extremely versatile. *Where did you get that?*
- **Llevo + gerund + time → present perfect (continuous) + for:** *Llevo dos años trabajando aquí* → *I've been working here **for** two years.*
- **Love / like + to-infinitive or -ing are both correct:** *I love to mix drinks* = *I love mixing drinks.* But never a bare infinitive: ❌ ~~I like go to the cinema~~ → ✅ *I like to go to the cinema.*
- **Accent is countable:** *My boss has **a** British accent* — not just "has accent".
- **Much (uncountable) vs. many (countable):** *How can you drink so **much** beer?* vs. *How can you drink so **many** glasses of beer?*

sections.title: 2. Phrasal Verbs with 'Put'
sections.content:
With phrasal verbs, **the secret is in the preposition, not the verb** — the same base verb creates totally different meanings depending on the particle.

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **put out** | to extinguish (separable) | *He put out the fire. He put it out with a wet cloth.* |
| **put on** ↔ **take off** | to dress / wear ↔ to remove clothing | *Do you put on your left shoe first?* |
| **put into** | to insert (always implies movement) | *You put the key into the lock.* |
| **put up with** | to tolerate (almost always used in the negative) | *I can't put up with my neighbors.* |
| **put down** / **write down** / **jot down** | to note something on paper | *Put it down on paper if you have a good idea.* |
| **put away** | to store something in its proper place | *Put your toys away before bed.* |
| **put back** | to return something to where it was | *Put the books back on the shelf.* |
| **put off** | to postpone | *I put the class off by 30 minutes.* |

**Notes:**

- Literal *"put up"* (e.g. *put the drinks up in the fridge*) isn't technically a phrasal verb by definition — a true phrasal verb creates a *new* meaning, which is exactly what *put up **with*** does.
- **Grease fire safety:** never put water on a grease fire — it spreads the flames. Use a cloth to put it out instead.

sections.title: 3. Interrogative Challenge — What vs. How (The Five Senses)
sections.content:
**What + verb + like → asks for a comparison** (needs *like*):

> *What does it **look** like? · What does it **sound** like? · What does it **taste** like? · What does it **smell** like? · What does it **feel** like?*

**How + verb → asks for an opinion / description** (uses adjectives, never *like*):

> *How does it **look**? · How does it **sound**? · How does it **taste**? · How does it **smell**? · How does it **feel**?*

> ❌ ~~How does it look like?~~ — **how** and **like** never go together.

| Answer | Question |
|---|---|
| It sounds like a locomotive. | What does it sound like? |
| It sounds great. | How does it sound? |
| It tastes like orange juice. | What does it taste like? |
| It tastes very sweet. | How does it taste? |
| It looks like a medieval castle. | What does it look like? |
| It smells like cheap perfume. | What does it smell like? |
| It feels like rabbit fur. | What does it feel like? |

**General interrogative reminder — auxiliary verbs are always required in questions and negatives, except when the main verb is *to be*:**

| Statement | Question |
|---|---|
| I'm talking to Peter. | Who are you talking to? |
| I went there yesterday. | When did you go there? |
| I've known him for six years. | How long have you known him? |

sections.title: 4. Grammar: Unless
sections.content:
**Unless** = *if...not* / *except if* — it flips an "only if" sentence into the negative.

> *I'll do it only if you support me.* → **I won't do it unless you support me.**

| Only if... | Unless... |
|---|---|
| He'll pay for it only if there's a proper invoice. | He won't pay for it unless there's a proper invoice. |
| I'll write the report only if you promise to sign it. | I won't write the report unless you promise to sign it. |
| I'll call the meeting only if at least 10 managers attend. | I won't call the meeting unless at least 10 managers attend. |
| I'll fly there only if you pay for my accommodation. | I won't fly there unless you pay for my accommodation. |
| I'll arrange the party only if you promise to stay sober. | I won't arrange the party unless you promise to stay sober. |

**Position:** *unless* usually sits in the middle of the sentence, but it can also start a sentence — less common, but correct:

> *Unless you come with me, I won't go to the party.*

title: English with Kyle
topic: Business Letter: Subscription Renewal · Fall Behind / Keep Up

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Dimos por supuesto que lo sabías. | We took for granted that you knew it. |
| No deberías burlarte de esa gente. | You shouldn't make fun of those people. |
| Hay espacio para uno más. | There's room / there's space for one more. |
| Las cortinas prendieron fuego. | The curtains caught fire. |
| Nosotros rellenaremos esos recuadros. | We'll fill in those boxes. |
| ¿Podrías dar marcha atrás unos metros? | Could you back up a few meters? |
| Mantén la espalda recta. | Keep your back straight. |
| Podemos descartar esa posibilidad. | We can rule out that possibility. |
| ¿Ha habido algún incidente últimamente? | Have there been any incidents lately? |

**Key notes:**

- **To take for granted** = dar por sentado — *We took for granted (that) you knew it.* (*that* is optional)
- **To make fun of** = burlarse de — *You shouldn't make fun of those people.*
- **To catch fire** = prenderse fuego — *The curtains caught fire.*
- **Fill in vs. fill out:** *fill in* the individual boxes/blanks · *fill out* a whole document/form.
- **To back up** = dar marcha atrás — *Could you back up a few meters?* (meters is countable → *a few meters*)
- **Possessives with body parts:** Spanish uses the definite article (*la espalda*), English uses the possessive: *keep **your** back straight*, not *the back*.
- **To rule out** = descartar — *You can rule out that possibility.*
- **Present perfect with *lately / recently / so far*:** *Have there been **any** incidents lately?* — use *any* when asking about existence.

sections.title: 2. Business Letter: Subscription Renewal ★ Main topic
sections.content:
### Letter

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Querido lector, | Dear reader, |
| Como probablemente sabrá, su suscripción anual de News Weekly termina al final de este mes. | As you may be aware, your annual subscription to News Weekly ends at the end of this month. |
| Hemos notado que todavía no ha renovado esta suscripción. | We've noticed that you haven't renewed your subscription yet. |
| Para asegurarse de seguir recibiendo la entrega de la revista, tendrá que renovar antes del 31 de marzo. | To ensure you continue to receive delivery of the magazine, you will need to renew before the 31st of March. |
| Tiene usted dos opciones de renovación. | You have two renewal options. |
| En primer lugar, podría renovar durante 12 meses por 150 euros, lo cual le proporcionará un ahorro del 50% del precio normal. | Firstly, you could renew for 12 months at a price of 150 euros, which would give you a savings of 50% on the magazine's normal price. |
| O podría elegir la opción de renovación anual automática por 130 euros al año, lo cual le proporcionaría un ahorro del 60%. | Or you could choose the automatic annual renewal option for 130 euros a year, which would give you a savings of 60%. |
| Si elige usted esa segunda opción, le regalaremos un lápiz de memoria de 4 GB gratis. | If you choose the second option, we will give you a free 4 gigabyte memory stick as a gift. |
| Se puede renovar online en nuestra página web, o nos puede llamar al número directo que aparece más abajo, o si lo prefiere, puede rellenar el formulario y enviárnoslo junto con el pago. | You can renew online at our webpage, or you can phone us directly at the number that appears below, or if you prefer, you can fill out the form and send it back to us along with the payment. |
| Compruebe por favor que sus datos personales son correctos e indique su número de referencia de cliente y la fecha de vencimiento de su suscripción en toda correspondencia. | Please check that your personal details are correct and quote your customer reference number and expiry date in all correspondence. |
| Atentamente, | Yours sincerely, |

---

### Key phrases and vocabulary

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Como probablemente sabrá | **As you may be aware** / **As you may know** |
| Asegurarse | **To ensure** / **to make sure** |
| Fecha de vencimiento | **Expiry date** |
| Rellenar el formulario | **To fill out** the form |
| Como regalo | **As a gift** |
| Junto con el pago | **Along with the payment** |
| Indicar / citar | **To quote** *(quote your reference number)* |
| Toda correspondencia | **All correspondence** |

### Grammar notes

**Insure / Ensure / Assure — three different words:**
- **insure** (with an *i*) → to buy insurance: *insure your car*
- **ensure** (with an *e*) → to make certain something happens: *to ensure you continue to receive the magazine* — synonym: **to make sure**
- **assure** (with an *a*) → to tell someone something is true, to reassure: *I assure you it's true*

**During vs. for:**
- **during** + a noun/period → *during the war · during the match*
- **for** + a duration → *I was there **for** a week* (not ~~during a week~~)

**Dates:** *the 31st of March* = *March 31st* — both correct.

**Expiry date** — when something (a subscription, a document, food) expires. With food, English often says the **best before date** instead.

sections.title: 3. Phrasal Verbs: Fall Behind / Keep Up
sections.content:
**To fall behind** = quedarse atrás (not separable — never *fall it behind*)

> *My daughter has fallen behind in her studies due to her illness.*
> *I'm worried about falling behind on my mortgage payments.*
> *The athlete has fallen behind with two laps to go.* *(to go = remaining)*

You can strengthen it with **well**: *He has fallen **well** behind.*

---

**To keep up (with)** = mantener el ritmo / mantenerse al día / no quedarse atrás (not separable — never *keep him up* in this sense)

> *Do you keep up with the news when you travel?*
> *He'll never be able to keep up with those Kenyan runners.*
> *Are you able to keep up with all this new technology?*
> *It's hard to keep up with all the latest developments in artificial intelligence.*

**Keep up** can also mean *seguir haciendo algo* (keep + gerund): *We can't keep stopping like this.*

**Keep it up** = a fixed expression meaning *keep going, good job* — *Keep it up!*

> ❌ ~~keep up doing it~~ — just say *keep it up* or *keep doing it*.

sections.title: 4. Vocabulary: Stuffy
sections.content:
**Stuffy** = a room that feels heavy, uncomfortable, poorly ventilated.

> *The room is a bit stuffy.* / *The room is a little stuffy.*

Related word: **to stuff** = *rellenar / meter algo dentro forzándolo* — *to stuff something into a bag.*

title: Agility Accelerator

sections.title: 1. Common Irregular Verb Practice
sections.intro: Practice repeating each sentence yourself to master the most common English irregular verbs in the affirmative/negative simple past contrast pattern (*"I did X, but I didn't do Y"*).

items.text: **Be** — I was happy, but I wasn't satisfied.
items.speak: I was happy, but I wasn't satisfied.
items.secondary: Ser — Fui feliz, pero no estaba satisfecho.

items.text: **Begin** — They began the project, but they didn't begin the presentation.
items.speak: They began the project, but they didn't begin the presentation.
items.secondary: Comenzar — Ellos comenzaron el proyecto, pero no comenzaron la presentación.

items.text: **Break** — I broke the glass, but I didn't break the plate.
items.speak: I broke the glass, but I didn't break the plate.
items.secondary: Romper — Rompí el vaso, pero no rompí el plato.

items.text: **Bring** — He brought his friend, but he didn't bring his sister.
items.speak: He brought his friend, but he didn't bring his sister.
items.secondary: Traer — Él trajo a su amigo, pero no trajo a su hermana.

items.text: **Build** — We built a house, but we didn't build a garage.
items.speak: We built a house, but we didn't build a garage.
items.secondary: Construir — Construimos una casa, pero no construimos un garaje.

items.text: **Buy** — She bought a car, but she didn't buy a bike.
items.speak: She bought a car, but she didn't buy a bike.
items.secondary: Comprar — Ella compró un coche, pero no compró una bicicleta.

items.text: **Catch** — I caught the ball, but I didn't catch the frisbee.
items.speak: I caught the ball, but I didn't catch the frisbee.
items.secondary: Atrapar — Atrapé la pelota, pero no atrapé el frisbee.

items.text: **Choose** — They chose the red dress, but they didn't choose the blue one.
items.speak: They chose the red dress, but they didn't choose the blue one.
items.secondary: Elegir — Ellos eligieron el vestido rojo, pero no eligieron el azul.

items.text: **Come** — He came to the party, but he didn't come to the meeting.
items.speak: He came to the party, but he didn't come to the meeting.
items.secondary: Venir — Él vino a la fiesta, pero no vino a la reunión.

items.text: **Cut** — She cut her hair, but she didn't cut her nails.
items.speak: She cut her hair, but she didn't cut her nails.
items.secondary: Cortar — Ella cortó su cabello, pero no cortó sus uñas.

items.text: **Do** — I did my homework, but I didn't do my chores.
items.speak: I did my homework, but I didn't do my chores.
items.secondary: Hacer — Hice mi tarea, pero no hice mis quehaceres.

items.text: **Drink** — They drank the juice, but they didn't drink the milk.
items.speak: They drank the juice, but they didn't drink the milk.
items.secondary: Beber — Ellos bebieron el jugo, pero no bebieron la leche.

items.text: **Drive** — He drove to work, but he didn't drive to the store.
items.speak: He drove to work, but he didn't drive to the store.
items.secondary: Conducir — Él condujo al trabajo, pero no condujo a la tienda.

items.text: **Eat** — We ate the pizza, but we didn't eat the salad.
items.speak: We ate the pizza, but we didn't eat the salad.
items.secondary: Comer — Comimos la pizza, pero no comimos la ensalada.

items.text: **Fall** — She fell on the ice, but she didn't fall on the stairs.
items.speak: She fell on the ice, but she didn't fall on the stairs.
items.secondary: Caer — Ella cayó en el hielo, pero no cayó en las escaleras.

items.text: **Feel** — I felt the heat, but I didn't feel the cold.
items.speak: I felt the heat, but I didn't feel the cold.
items.secondary: Sentir — Sentí el calor, pero no sentí el frío.

items.text: **Find** — They found the keys, but they didn't find the wallet.

items.speak: She forgot her purse, but she didn't forget her phone.

items.text: **Get** — He got the job, but he didn't get the promotion.

items.text: **Go** — I went to the park, but I didn't go to the museum.

items.text: **Have** — We had a picnic, but we didn't have a barbecue.

items.text: **Hear** — He heard the music, but he didn't hear the conversation.

items.secondary: Oír — Él oyó la música, pero no oyó la conversación.

items.text: **Hide** — She hid the key, but she didn't hide the money.

items.text: **Know** — I knew the answer, but I didn't know the question.

items.text: **Say** — They said goodbye, but they didn't say hello.

items.secondary: Decir — Ellos dijeron adiós, pero no dijeron hola.

items.text: **See** — He saw the movie, but he didn't see the trailer.

items.text: **Sell** — She sold the car, but she didn't sell the house.

sections.title: 5. Such + Irregular Verbs

Listen and repeat until the structure **such a/an + adjective + noun** feels automatic with the present perfect (*I've never had...*).

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No estuviste donde yo estuve. | You weren't where I was. |
| No hiciste lo que yo hice. | You didn't do what I did. |

| Toma libre el resto del día. | Take the rest of the day off. |
| Hace falta mucho más que eso. | It takes much more than that. |

| Es una poción para los calvos. | It's a potion for bald people / for the bald. |

| Ya tenemos un pedido de China. | We already have an order from China. |
| Tenemos que embarcar un millón de frascos para dentro de un mes. | We need to ship a million bottles within a month. |
| ¿Los tenéis en stock? | Do you have them in stock? |
| No los hemos empezado a fabricar aún. | We haven't started producing them yet. |
| ¿Estáis locos? ¿Cómo vais a fabricarlos? | You're crazy. How are you going to produce them? |
| Por eso te he llamado. | That's why I called you. |
| ¿Qué tengo que ver yo con esto? | What do I have to do with this? |
| Pensé que a lo mejor querías ayudarnos. | I thought you might want to help us. |
| ¿Ayudaros a hacer qué? | Help you do what? |
| A financiar la producción. | To finance the production. |
| ¿Desde cuándo soy yo un banco? | Since when am I a bank? |
| Pero tienes mucho dinero, hombre. | But you have a lot of money. |
| Pero no para tus locas ideas. | But not for your crazy ideas. |
| ¿Sabes cuántos chinos son calvos? | Do you know how many Chinese people are bald? |
| 340 millones de chinos querrán nuestro producto. | 340 million Chinese people will want our product. |
| Multiplica eso por tres euros por frasco. | Multiply that by three euros per bottle. |
| ¿Cuánto dinero crees que necesitaréis? | How much money do you think you'll need? |
| 80.000 pavos. | 80,000 bucks. |
| Bueno, veré lo que puedo hacer. | Well, I'll see what I can do. |
| Pero estás forrado. | But you're filthy rich. |
| Puedes conseguir el dinero en una hora. | You can get the money in an hour. |
| El dinero no crece en los árboles. | Money doesn't grow on trees. |

**Key notes:**

- **Hace falta** = it takes / it's necessary — built with the verb *to take*: *Hace falta mucho más que eso* → *It takes much more than that.*
- **Reflexive "a sí mismo"** = itself — *Se vende a sí mismo* → *It sells itself.*
- **Phrasal verb "take ... off" (separable):** *Take the rest of the day off* — not ~~take off the rest of the day~~.
- **Por eso** = that's why — *Por eso te he llamado* → *That's why I called you.*
- **Tener que ver con** = to have to do with — *¿Qué tengo que ver yo con esto?* → *What do I have to do with this?*
- **Money slang:** *pavos* = **bucks** (US English); the British say **quid**. *80,000 bucks.*
- **Embarcar** = to ship; **forrado** = filthy rich.

sections.title: 2. Conditional Advice: If I Were You
sections.content:
**Structure:** *If I were you, I would / wouldn't + [infinitive]* = *Yo en tu lugar...* / *Yo que tú...*

This is second conditional advice — after *if I were you*, the modal is always **would**, no matter who the subject is.

| Situation | Advice |
|---|---|
| I'm planning to invest my money in antiques. | If I were you, I wouldn't invest my money in antiques. |
| I'm thinking about holding a Christmas party outdoors. | If I were you, I wouldn't hold a Christmas party outdoors — too cold. |
| I'm thinking about giving my brother a stapler for Christmas. | If I were you, I wouldn't give my brother a stapler for Christmas. |
| I'm thinking of taking my girlfriend to an English restaurant. | If I were you, I wouldn't take her to an English restaurant — the English aren't known for their food. |
| I'm going to Canada on Thursday. | If I were you, I would visit the East Coast. / I would go camping. / I wouldn't bring a heavy jacket in the summer. / I would pack extra boots. |

**Grammar note:** *If I were you* always uses **were** (not *was*) for every subject — this is the classic subjunctive form used in second conditional sentences.

sections.title: 3. Passive Voice Review
sections.content:
**Structure:** [subject] + **to be** (conjugated in the same tense as the active sentence) + past participle (+ *by* + agent)

> *"We're changing the voice, not the tense."*

### Active → Passive drills

| Active | Passive |
|---|---|
| Someone told me to wait here. | I was told to wait here. |
| Someone asked them to be quiet. | They were asked to be quiet. |
| Someone informed me yesterday. | I was informed yesterday. |
| Someone should warn him about the danger. | He should be warned about the danger. |
| Anyone and everyone can trust him. | He can be trusted by anyone and everyone. |
| Someone must do it. | It must be done. |
| No one did it. | It wasn't done. |
| Someone should have done it last week. | It should have been done last week. |
| No one included you on the list. | You weren't included on the list. |
| No one invited you to the party. | You weren't invited to the party. |
| No one has contacted me yet. | I haven't been contacted yet. |
| They didn't develop a solution. | A solution wasn't developed. |
| He didn't know her name. | Her name wasn't known. |

### Spanish passive translations

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Siempre se hará a mano. | It will always be made by hand. |
| Debería hacerse a mano. | It should be made by hand. |
| ¿Cuándo se descubrió? | When was it discovered? |
| A veces se descubren cosas muy valiosas. | Sometimes very valuable things are discovered. |
| Estas listas deben estudiarse con cuidado. | These lists should be studied carefully. |

**Note:** Spanish *hacer* covers both *make* and *do*, so *hecho a mano* is usually **made by hand** in English, though *done by hand* also exists for other contexts.

sections.title: 4. Interrogative Drills: How Often vs. How Many Times
sections.content:
**Drill: I give you the answer, you ask the question.**

| Answer | Question |
|---|---|
| I feel like staying at home. | What do you feel like doing? |
| I feel afraid when I enter a hospital. | How do you feel when you enter a hospital? |
| I found it in the kitchen. | Where did you find it? |
| He finds his customers through advertising. | How does he find his customers? |
| You can find bargains in the Rastro. | Where can I find bargains? |
| The boy was found near the supermarket. | Where was the boy found? |
| The battle was fought nine miles east of Paris. | Where was the battle fought? |
| He flies to Paris twice a month. | How often does he fly to Paris? |
| I've flown to London twice this month. | How many times have you flown there this month? |
| I've forgotten it three times this month. | How many times have you forgotten it this month? |

**Grammar notes:**

- **How often?** asks for a *frequency* (con qué frecuencia). **How many times?** asks for a *count* of occasions (número de veces) — it doesn't have to be a habit.
- **find, found, found** (encontrar) vs. **found, founded, founded** (fundar): *Where was the boy **found**?* but *When was the company **founded**?*
- With an auxiliary verb (*does/did*), the main verb stays in the **infinitive**: *How often **does** he **fly**...?*, not ~~flies~~.

title: English with Kyle
topic: So That (Purpose Clauses) · The Verb "To Take": Four Uses · Although / However / Nevertheless / Plus

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Demasiadas cosas en mi escritorio. | Too many things on my desk. |
| Oí una voz extraña que me asustó. | I heard a strange voice that frightened me. |
| Miré atrás pero no vi nada. | I looked back, but I didn't see anything. |
| Miré en todas partes. | I looked everywhere. |
| Por fin me di cuenta de lo que era. | I finally realized what it was. |
| Creo que no vale la pena. | I don't think it's worth it. |
| O sea, no lo deberíamos hacer. | In other words, we shouldn't do it. |
| Es imposible que fracasemos. | It's impossible for us to fail. |
| ¿Cuál es vuestro secreto para el éxito? | What's your secret to success? |
| Hace falta mucho más que eso. | It takes a lot more than that. |

**Key notes:**

- **Darse cuenta** = to realize — *Me di cuenta de lo que era* → *I realized what it was.*
- **Frightened** = asustado, *in the moment* · **scared / afraid** = *tienes miedo de algo*, a general fear — *I'm afraid/scared of heights*, but *I got frightened* when I looked over the edge.
- **Impersonal structure:** *It's + adjective + for + subject + to + infinitive* — *Es imposible que fracasemos* → *It's impossible **for us to** fail*, not ~~it's impossible that we fail~~.
- **Hace falta** = it takes / it's necessary, built with the verb *to take*.

sections.title: 2. Grammar: So That (Purpose Clauses)
sections.content:
**Structure:** [idea] + **so that** + subject + modal (can/could/will/would/won't) + infinitive = *para que*

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Trabajo para poder mantenerte. | I work so that I can support you. |
| Tengo un paraguas para poder quedarme seco bajo la lluvia. | I have an umbrella so that I can stay dry in the rain. |
| Vine para que tú me ayudaras. | I came so that you could help me. |
| Habla alto para que todos te oigan. | Speak loud so that everyone can hear you. |

### Student examples from class

- *I study so that I can speak English fluently and confidently.*
- *I have my phone so that I can send messages.*
- *I have a computer so that I can send emails.*
- *I have a book so that I can read on the plane.*
- *I have this microphone so that you can hear me.*
- *I bought a flat so that I could avoid paying rent.*
- *I set the clock so that I would arrive on time.*
- *I saved some money so that we can go on vacation.*
- *I took a shower so that I wouldn't feel so hot.*

**Grammar notes:**

- **Always needs a new subject** after *so that*: *so that I can · so that you could · so that we won't*.
- ❌ ~~so that avoid~~ — you can't drop the subject + modal: *so that I could **avoid**...*
- Don't use *so that* to mean *because*: ❌ ~~I feel heat so that I took a shower~~ → ✅ *I took a shower **because** I felt hot* / *I took a shower **so that** I wouldn't feel so hot.*
- **In order to** + infinitive is a more formal alternative — but only works when the subject **doesn't change**.
- Using this structure correctly helps you avoid the classic mistake of saying ~~for to~~.

sections.title: 3. Vocabulary: To Be Worth It
sections.content:
**Creo que no vale la pena** → **I don't think it's worth it.**

- ❌ ~~it doesn't worthy~~ / ❌ ~~it isn't worthy~~ — *worthy* is **not** used this way.
- *I think it isn't worth it* is grammatically fine, but **"I don't think it's worth it"** (negating the main verb *think*) is far more common and natural in English.
- **Negative transportation:** Spanish can negate the subordinate clause (*Creo que no iré a la fiesta*), but English usually moves the negation to the main verb: *Creo que no iré a la fiesta* → **I don't think I will go to the party** (not ~~I think I won't go~~).

> *Would you like to go on a trip to China for 5,000 euros?* — **I don't think it's worth it. Too expensive.**

sections.title: 4. Verb "To Take": Four Uses
sections.content:
From Kyle's book *"The Verb Circus: Los verbos esenciales del inglés"* (also in the resource center, with audio challenges for each use).

### The four main uses of "to take"

1. **tomar** (physical taking / consuming) → *to take a bus/train · to take a pill/medication · to take a seat*
   - ⚠ *tomar un café* ≠ ~~take a coffee~~ — say **to have a coffee**
2. **llevar** (a person somewhere, or an object with you) → *I took my girlfriend to the cinema* · *I always take my phone with me*
3. **tardar** (duration) → *it takes* + time — *How long does it take? It takes about five hours to drive from Madrid to Barcelona.*
4. **hacer falta** (necessity) → *it takes* = it requires — *It takes a lot of effort. It's going to take money.*

### Song reference: "I've Got My Mind Set on You" (George Harrison)

- *"It's going to take time, a whole lot of precious time... it's going to take money, plenty of money"* → *va a hacer falta tiempo / dinero*
- **to be set on (something)** = estar decidido/determinado — *I'm set on it* = I'm determined

**Fixed expression:** *No lo tomes así* → **Don't take it that way** = don't interpret it that way.

sections.title: 5. Grammar: Short Answers (Yes/No + Subject + Auxiliary)
sections.content:
**Structure:** Yes/No, + subject + auxiliary — don't repeat the full verb.

| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| Do you live in Spain? | Yes, I do. |
| Are you Spanish? | Yes, I am. |
| Is Mexico in Europe? | No, it isn't. |
| Would you like to be a millionaire? | Yes, I would. |
| Will you be here tomorrow? | Yes, I will. |
| Did you see a good movie last week? | Yes, I did. |
| Do your neighbors give you a lot of problems? | No, they don't. |
| Could you speak English when you were five years old? | No, I couldn't. |
| Does it rain a lot in Spain? | No, it doesn't. |
| Are your shoes clean? | Yes, they are. |
| Does your back give you a lot of trouble? | No, it doesn't. |
| Does Spain belong to the European Union? | Yes, it does. |
| Do the people in Chile speak Chinese? | No, they don't. |
| Are you from Finland? | No, I'm not. |
| Was there a fire in your house yesterday? | No, there wasn't. |

**The key skill:** listen carefully for **which auxiliary** the question uses (*do/does, is/are, will, would, could, did, was/were...*) and echo that same one back — don't default to *do/don't* for everything.

sections.title: 6. Grammar: Contrast & Addition Conjunctions
sections.content:
### Although / Even though

- Essentially the same meaning; **even though** is a little more emphatic about the contrast.
- Can start the sentence **or** sit mid-sentence: *Although it was raining cats and dogs, he took a walk in the park.* / *He took a walk in the park although it was raining cats and dogs.*
- *Although interest rates are high, Aki is going to ask for a loan.* / *Even though interest rates are high, Aki is going to ask for a loan.*
- ⚠ Modals never take *to*: ❌ ~~even though we will to start~~

### ...but... anyway / ...but... in any case

- *It was raining cats and dogs, but he took a walk in the park **anyway**.*
- **in any case** is the least common of the three alternatives (although / even though / anyway).

### However vs. Nevertheless

- **However** → usually **positive** idea, however, **negative** idea: *Luigi has important business in Stuttgart, however, he delegates it to Anna.*
- **Nevertheless** → usually **negative** idea, nevertheless, **positive** idea: *It was raining cats and dogs, nevertheless, we still had a great time.*
- *Ronny's father is rich, however, Ronny never has any money.* (positive, however, negative)
- *He lost his job. Nevertheless, he won the lottery.* (negative, nevertheless, positive)

### Plus

- Builds **in one direction** — adds a further point, usually with **three or more** items in the same direction (all positive or all negative).
- *It's beautiful, plus the food is great.* (positive, positive, plus positive)
- *It's very expensive, and plus, the color is terrible.* (negative, negative, plus negative)
- Can say either **"plus"** or **"and plus"** — both work in most cases.

**Aside:** *"It's raining cats and dogs"* is a textbook expression Kyle rarely uses in real speech — more natural: **"it's pouring."**

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Cuándo lanzaremos la campaña de prensa? | When will we launch the advertising campaign? |
| Esto podría haber sido peor. | This could have been worse. |
| Quiero un estudio en profundidad. | I need an in-depth study. |
| En cuanto a él, puedes hacer lo que quieras. | As far as he's concerned, you can do whatever you want. |
| Se comporta como si fuera el jefe. | He acts as if he were the boss. |
| Soy partidario de ir en coche. | I'm in favor of going by car. |
| Han ocurrido bastantes cosas desde entonces. | Quite a few things have happened since then. |
| Hay bastante agua en el vaso. | There's quite a lot of water in the glass. |

**Key notes:**

- **Worse** (comparative) vs **the worst** (superlative, needs *the*): *I am worse at tennis than my neighbor, but my uncle is **the** worst.*
- **Compound adjectives need a hyphen:** *an **in-depth** study.*
- **As far as he's concerned** needs the verb *is* — not ~~as far as he concerned~~. Also: *as for him*.
- **Subjunctive "were" after "as if":** *He acts **as if he were** the boss* (never *was*, same rule as *if I were you*).
- **In favor of** is a preposition → followed by a gerund: *I'm in favor of **going** by car*, not ~~of go~~.
- **Word order with *haber*:** Spanish *han ocurrido bastantes cosas* (verb first) becomes **quite a few things have happened** in English — the subject comes first, no dummy *there*.

sections.title: 2. Vocabulary: Launching a Campaign (Kick Off / Launch / Release)
sections.content:
**Kick off** comes from football: the ball starts on the center dot, and the players *kick it off*. It's used for the official start of a project, a campaign, or even a regular meeting.

This is a good example of a wider pattern: prepositions and phrasal verbs often make more sense once you know their **opposite** — *up ↔ down*, *in ↔ out*, *over ↔ under*, *on ↔ off* (*turn it on / turn it off*). Understanding the opposite unlocks the meaning.

**Launch vs. release vs. kick off:**

- **to launch** a campaign/product — pushing something out to the public (paying for it, promoting it): *When will we launch the advertising campaign?*
- **to release** an album/movie — something simply *becomes available/accessible* to the public: *You release a movie · it becomes released*
- **to kick off** a campaign/project/meeting — the official starting moment (from football); can also be used loosely for something as small as a regular meeting starting

**Spelling:** cam**paign** (C-A-M-P-A-I-G-N) — not *camping*.

**Gig** = un trabajo / un bolo — an informal word for a job or contract (can also mean a small concert): *Teaching in Vodafone was a good gig.*

sections.title: 3. Grammar: Not As Much / Not As Many (Fewer & Less)
sections.content:
**Structure:** **fewer** ↔ **not as many** (plural countable) · **less** ↔ **not as much** (uncountable)

| Fewer / Less | Not as many / Not as much |
|---|---|
| There are fewer people in Madrid than there are in Tokyo. | There are not as many people in Madrid as there are in Tokyo. |
| There's less sunlight in Norway than there is in Spain. | There's not as much sunlight in Norway as there is in Spain. |
| There are fewer factories in Bulgaria than there are in England. | There are not as many factories in Bulgaria as there are in England. |
| There are fewer camels in Spain than there are in Egypt. | There are not as many camels in Spain as there are in Egypt. |
| There's less sand in Luxembourg than there is in Egypt. | There's not as much sand in Luxembourg as there is in Egypt. |

### Student examples from class

- *There are fewer languages spoken in North America than there are in Africa.* / *There are not as many languages spoken in North America as there are in Africa.*
- *Is there as much pollution in Palma as there is in Beijing?* → *There isn't as much pollution in Palma as there is in Beijing.*
- *Are there as many cars in London as there are in New York?* → *There aren't as many cars in London as there are in New York.*
- *There aren't as many taxis in my town as there are in Barcelona.*
- *There are fewer fish in the Mediterranean than in the Cantabrian Sea.*

### From the Agility Accelerator (superlative comparisons)

- *I'm not as rich as the richest person in China.*
- *I'm not as tall as the tallest man in Belgium.*
- *My phone isn't more expensive than the most expensive phone in Japan.*
- *I'm not as athletic as the most athletic person in Spain. · I'm not as fast as the fastest runner in Ethiopia.*
- *There aren't as many robots in Spanish public buildings as there are in Japan.*
- *Young people today read fewer books than when I was young.*
- *It rains quite a lot in Germany, but not as much as it does in the UK.*

sections.title: 4. Vocabulary: Quantifiers — A Few / Quite A Few / Only A Few
sections.content:
| Quantifier | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|
| **few** | hay pocos — implies scarcity, almost none | *There are few Japanese people in Madrid* (very few) |
| **a few** | hay algunos — some, neutral-to-positive | *There are a few Eskimos in Madrid* (more than zero, maybe more than expected) |
| **quite a few** | bastantes — a considerable number (countable) | *There are quite a few places to go bowling* |
| **only a few** | muy pocos / limitados — emphasizes limitation | *There are only a few places to go indoor skiing in Spain* |
| **quite a lot of** | considerablemente — countable **or** uncountable | *It's quite hot* |

**"A lot of" is the safest all-purpose quantifier** — it works with countable and uncountable nouns, and in affirmative, negative, and interrogative sentences. It always works.

sections.title: 5. Grammar: Used To / Get Used To / Be Used To
sections.content:
**Three structures, three meanings:**

- **used to** + infinitive → past habit, no longer true: *I used to live in a small town.*
- **to be used to** + -ing/noun → estar acostumbrado a (already accustomed): *Peter is used to living well.*
- **to get used to** + -ing/noun → becoming accustomed, a transition: *It took me a long time to get used to Spanish food.*

**Accustomed to** is a more formal synonym for *(be) used to* — same meaning, higher register: *Peter is accustomed to living well* = *Peter is used to living well.*

**"To get" here means llegar a ser (to become)** — same pattern as *to get tired* (cansarse), *to get wet* (mojarse), *to get better* (mejorarse), *to get sick*, *to get dark*.

### Drills (accustomed to → used to)

- *Peter is accustomed to living well.* → **Peter is used to living well.**
- *Ronnie is accustomed to asking his father for money.* → **Ronnie is used to asking his father for money.**
- *It took me a long time to get accustomed to Spanish food.* → **It took me a long time to get used to Spanish food.**
- *Aki is getting accustomed to working in Louisiana.* → **Aki is getting used to working in Louisiana.**
- *Nancy is accustomed to dealing with a lot of different people.* → **Nancy is used to dealing with a lot of different people.**
- *I can't get accustomed to the heat.* → **I can't get used to the heat.**
- *You'll understand me better once you get accustomed to my accent.* → **...once you get used to my accent.**

sections.title: 6. Interrogative Challenge: Which vs. Where & Whose
sections.content:
**Which vs. where:** use **which** when choosing among a **defined, limited** set of options; use **where** for a general, open-ended location.

> *They went that way.* → **Which way did they go?** *(a specific direction is already implied)*
> compare: *They went to the store.* → **Where did they go?** *(general)*

**Whose + noun, immediately together** — the verb *to be* always comes **after** the noun, never right after *whose*:

- ❌ ~~Whose is that?~~ / ~~Whose those cigarettes?~~
- ✅ *Those cigarettes are Frank's.* → **Whose cigarettes are those?**
- ✅ *I took Bill's umbrella.* → **Whose umbrella did you take?**
- ✅ *We're going to use Eddie's car.* → **Whose car are we going to use?**

### More drills

- *The trial lasted three weeks.* → **How long did the trial last?**
- *I'll be back in 20 minutes.* → **When will you be back?**
- *You should turn over the omelet when I tell you.* → **When should I turn over the omelet?**
- *I want you to use the red car, not the blue car.* → **Which car do you want me to use?**
- *I take aspirin when I have a headache.* → **What do you take when you have a headache?** — stress and intonation matter here: the same word order can sound like a statement or a question, in both English and Spanish.

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
A dark little story, told sentence by sentence:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Un hombre entró en un callejón. | A man walked into an alley. |
| Era de noche. | It was nighttime. |
| Se acercó andando a tres hombres. | He walked up to three men. |
| Les enseñó algo que llevaba en una caja. | He showed them something he had in a box. |
| ¿Qué es lo que buscaban? | What were they looking for? |
| Buscaban un brazo. | They were looking for an arm. |
| ¿Por qué me cuentas historias como esa? | Why do you tell me stories like that? |
| Creía que te gustaban. | I thought you liked them. |
| Me ponen los pelos de punta. | They make my hair stand on end. |
| Hablemos de cosas más agradables, pero primero termina el relato. | Let's talk about nicer things, but first finish the story. |
| Para resumirlo, se trataba de un médico. | To sum it up, it was about a doctor. |
| El que llevaba la caja era médico. | The one carrying the box was a doctor. |
| Dos días antes se había cortado el brazo. | Two days before, he had cut off his arm. |
| Fue a enseñarlo a los tres hombres — así cumplía una promesa. | He went to show it to the three men — that way he fulfilled a promise. |
| Los cuatro hombres se conocían. | The four men knew each other. |
| Se conocieron en un barco que se hundió. | They met on a ship that sank. |
| Fueron los únicos supervivientes. | They were the only survivors. |
| Lograron llegar a una isla desierta. | They managed to reach a desert island. |
| No había comida en la isla. | There was no food on the island. |
| Sabían que morirían de hambre si no... | They knew they would starve to death if they didn't... |
| Ya puedes dejar de contar la historia. | You can stop telling the story now. |
| Ya me imagino lo que pasó. | I can imagine what happened. |

**Key notes:**

- **walk/drive/run up to** = acercarse (a physical approach, implies motion toward something): *I drove up to the window · I ran up to the police officer.*
- **cut** (herirse/cortarse, superficial) vs. **cut off** (amputar, completely severed): *I cut my finger* vs. *He cut off his arm.*
- English uses possessive pronouns where Spanish uses the definite article with body parts: **his arm**, not ~~the arm~~.
- **each other** (el uno al otro, reciprocal) vs. **myself/ourselves** (reflexive): *The four men knew each other.*
- **manage to** + infinitive = lograr + infinitivo: *They managed to reach a desert island.*
- **Boat vs. ship** (Uncle Walt's rule): *"You can put a boat on a ship, but you can't put a ship on a boat."* — a boat is smaller/carried; a ship is the larger vessel.
- **shipwreck** = the wrecked ship once it's at the bottom of the ocean; **it sank** = the event of sinking (survivable, as in this story).

sections.title: 2. Grammar: To Be Worth — Full Review
sections.content:
**Structure:** *to be worth* + [noun / amount / gerund]

- **Worth + noun/amount:** *This pen is worth a euro. · A kilogram of gold is worth more than a kilogram of silver.*
- **Worth + gerund:** since *worth* needs a noun, a verb becomes a gerund-noun: *It's worth studying. · That book is worth buying. · English is worth knowing. · It's not worth getting upset about such a little thing.*

### [amount] worth of [thing] — por valor de

Uses the Saxon genitive ('s): *five **euros' worth of** candy* = *chuches por valor de cinco euros.*

- *I bought five euros worth of candy.*
- *The company bought a million euros worth of software.*
- *They came back with 3,000 euros worth of furniture.*
- *I bought about 30 euros worth of groceries this afternoon.*

### Worth vs. Worthy — a common confusion

- **worth** = *vale* — the **value** something has (financial or emotional/sentimental): *It's worth a lot to me* (even if it only cost 50 cents — *to be worth* is subjective, not the same as *cuánto vale/cuesta*).
- **worthy** = *digno (de)* — **deserving**, an adjective: *He won the prize because he was worthy · the most worthy team won.* Often compound: **prize-worthy**, **praiseworthy**, **Oscar-worthy**, **World-Cup-worthy**.

### Worthwhile — a general synonym for "merece la pena"

- *It's worthwhile visiting Egypt.* / *Visiting Egypt is worthwhile.*
- Strengthen it with **well**: *It's **well worthwhile** getting there early.*

### Worth my/your/his while — a possessive idiom

- *It isn't worth my while leaving at 6:00 if I'm going to hit a lot of traffic.* *(to hit traffic = encontrarse con tráfico)*
- *I'll make it worth your while* — often used in business/negotiation: offering an incentive.

### Worthless

- *que no tiene valor* — *She paid a lot of money for a vase that turned out to be worthless.*
- *Without the original frame, that picture is worthless.*

sections.title: 3. Interrogative Challenge: Passive & Time Questions
sections.content:
**Passive and time-based question drills** — I give you the answer, you ask the question:

| Answer | Question |
|---|---|
| My kids are playing with my brother's son. | Who are your kids playing with? |
| They weren't ready because they overslept. | Why weren't they ready? |
| He will be promoted next month. | When will he be promoted? |
| The meeting will be held in the boardroom. | Where will the meeting be held? |
| You should go by taxi. | How should I go? |
| You can go whenever you want. | When can I go? |
| The train left the station at 2:00. | What time did the train leave the station? |
| This pen is John's. | Whose pen is this? |

**Grammar notes:**

- **to oversleep** (accidental, a mistake — the alarm didn't go off) vs. **to sleep in** (staying in bed longer than usual, can be intentional, e.g. on a Saturday).
- **to hold a meeting / the meeting will be held** = tener lugar (passive voice + question word).
- **Whose + noun** stays together, immediately: *Whose pen is this?* — never ~~whose is this pen~~.
